answers.text: Tell it to always give back the same three lines, same order: date, item and quantity, then any change. Line one is the date alone, line two is item and quantity together, line three is the change or 'none'. If nothing changed, write 'none' on that line instead of leaving it blank or guessing.
Ask for one line per claim — date, amount, category, submitter — with a total at the bottom. The total should be all the listed amounts added together for the week.

Something in the dates here doesn't add up. It calls the 19th three days out, but the call was on the 14th — that's five days, not three. One of those two numbers, the date or the day-count, doesn't match the other.

The 62 versus 54 works out to about 15%, so that bit's fine. But 3 late out of 62 works out closer to 95%, not the 97% it says. It also says stock held steady at 340 units even though deliveries were up 15%, with no explanation.
I'd sign off Output 2 — it shows its working. Output 1 doesn't say what the actual sales or returns figures were. It could be correct, but there's no way to check it as it stands.

I'd send Reply 2 — it's got the order number and credit reference in it. Reply 1 just says 'entirely our error' without saying how anyone knows that. Reply 1 might well be accurate, I'd just want to see it checked first.

1. No — that's the customer's own address, personal data with no reason to run through an unvetted tool.
2. Yes — an aggregate figure like this carries nothing identifiable.
3. No — it's still internal and not public, so it stays out.
4. Yes — it's already out there publicly, no added risk.
5. No — that's a colleague's personal number, no business need to share it here.

I'd hold back the unit pricing and discounts rather than paste them straight in. That clause naming both parties by name makes me want to leave it out as well. The delivery schedule and registration details seem low-risk, I'd paste those as they are.

I'd add a step where someone checks the totals against the system before it goes out. It happens just before the report is sent up, not at some point earlier. It's built to catch a number that's actually off, not just a typo.

Step 1, where it reads the order and pulls the items, is where a mistake would start. Step 4 is the one that needs a gate, since that's when the email sends with no one looking. It should check the extracted quantities against the email and confirm stock is genuinely available.
